docs.text:
Generates a list of patterns indices (start index, stop index) randomly such that: - the patterns have a size in [min_width_pattern, max_width_patterns[ - the patterns do not overlap - the patterns indices stays within the total signal size

The algorithm is the following:

  1. Compute patterns size (uniformly between min_width_pattern and max_width_patterns).

  2. Split the total signal size into equal length segments. Each segment will contain exactly one pattern. So there are n_patterns segments.

  3. For each segment, choose uniformly the starting and end points of the pattern such that the patterns fits into the segment.

    """
    Generates a list of patterns indices (start index, stop index) randomly such that:
    - the patterns have a size in [min_width_pattern, max_width_patterns[
    - the patterns do not overlap
    - the patterns indices stays within the total signal size

    The algorithm is the following:

    1.  Compute patterns size (uniformly between min_width_pattern and max_width_patterns).

    2.  Split the total signal size into equal length segments.
        Each segment will contain exactly one pattern.
        So there are `n_patterns` segments.

    3.  For each segment, choose uniformly the starting and end points of the pattern such that the patterns fits into the segment.



    :param random_generator: a random generator
    :param signal_size: total signal size
    :param n_patterns: total number of patterns
    :param min_width_pattern: the minimal width of the patterns
    :param max_width_patterns: the maximal width of the patterns
    :return: a list of patterns indices (start index, stop index)
    """
    if n_patterns <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"the number of patterns should be greater than zero, got {n_patterns}")
    if max_width_patterns * n_patterns > signal_size:
        raise ValueError(
            'n_patterns times max_width_patterns should not exceed the total signal size '
            f'({max_width_patterns} * {n_patterns} > {signal_size})')
    # randomly generates sizes for all patterns
    patterns_sizes = random_generator.integers(low=min_width_pattern, high=max_width_patterns, size=n_patterns)
    # size of segments (for splitting the total signal length)
    segment_size = signal_size // n_patterns
    # compute patterns indices
    patterns_indices = []

    if n_patterns == 1:
        start = random_generator.integers(low=0, high=signal_size - patterns_sizes[0])
        end = start + patterns_sizes[0]
        patterns_indices += [(start, end)]
    else:
        for i in range(n_patterns - 1):
            start = random_generator.integers(low=i * segment_size, high=(i + 1) * segment_size - patterns_sizes[i])
            end = start + patterns_sizes[i]
            patterns_indices += [(start, end)]
        # take care of the last remaining segment
        i = n_patterns - 1
        start = random_generator.integers(low=i * segment_size, high=signal_size - patterns_sizes[i])
        end = start + patterns_sizes[i]
        patterns_indices += [(start, end)]
    return patterns_indices

def get_patterns_uniform_probability(random_generator: np.random.Generator, signal_size: int, n_patterns: int,
                                     min_width_pattern: int, max_width_patterns: int) -> np.array:
    """
    Generate a probability array (sum = 1) of size `signal_size` that contains `n_patterns` segments where the probability is constant and non-zero and the rest is zero.

    Useful for some events (e.g., values drop) in some region of time

    Example
    >>> get_patterns_uniform_probability(random_generator=np.random.default_rng(0), signal_size=10, n_patterns=2, min_width_pattern=2, max_width_patterns=3)
    ... np.array([0., 0., 0.25, 0.25, 0., 0., 0.25, 0.25, 0., 0.])

    :param random_generator: a random generator
    :param signal_size: total signal size
    :param n_patterns: total number of patterns
    :param min_width_pattern: the minimal width of the patterns
    :param max_width_patterns: the maximal width of the patterns
    :return: a numpy array of probabilities (sum = 1)
    """
    # generate indices for patterns (regions where the probabilities should be constant)
    patterns_indices = generate_random_patterns_indices(
        random_generator=random_generator,
        signal_size=signal_size,
        n_patterns=n_patterns,
        min_width_pattern=min_width_pattern,
        max_width_patterns=max_width_patterns
    )

    # initialize probability array with zeros
    p = np.zeros(signal_size)

    # set constant values for patterns regions
    for i, j in patterns_indices:
        p[i:j] = 1

    # normalize and return
    return p / sum(p)

docs.title: Chaining generators through pipelines¶
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to chain different generators using the provided Pipeline class.

Note: this Pipeline is not compatible with sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline.

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Compose several defect generators into one pipeline — select, add outliers, corrupt with noise, drop rows — applied in sequence to a single dataset.

docs.title: How a pipeline works¶
docs.text: A Pipeline is a small registry of steps. Each step pairs a name with a generator; calling generate walks the steps in insertion order, feeding each generator the output of the previous one. Parameters are passed once, in a params dict keyed by step name. The result is a chain of defects applied to a single dataset — closer to real dirty data than any single generator in isolation.

docs.title: The data¶
docs.text: Fake data from make_blobs (scikit-learn): four well-separated clusters. Generators act on tabular data only, so the class label travels inside X as a third column; a selector can then target it by its column position (2).

docs.title: Building the pipeline¶
docs.text:
Two steps:

  • imbalance — UndersamplingGenerator with a ClassSelector over the label column (position 2). The proportions are the shares of the total row count removed per class: class 0 loses only a few rows (0.05) while classes 2 and 3 are thinned out (0.15 and 0.2); selectors take int column positions, so no name mapping is needed.
  • noise — AdditiveNoiseGenerator with norm(scale=0.5): a small Gaussian perturbation added to every remaining cell, after rows are gone.

Order matters: noise after imbalance means noise is added to the surviving rows only. Swapping the steps would perturb rows that are later deleted.

docs.title: Inspecting the result¶
docs.text: In the scatter, look for the thinned clusters (classes 2 and 3 nearly gone) and slightly jittered positions from the noise step.

docs.title: Class counts before and after¶
docs.text: Class 0 dominates after the imbalance step; classes 2 and 3 keep only a handful of rows.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• A pipeline stores steps (name, generator, params) and applies them in insertion order.
  • Each step's generator must match the pipeline's data type (tabular here).
  • Later steps act on the output of earlier steps — order matters.
  • params is keyed by step name — renaming a step means renaming its params entry.

import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP

# DGP definition (linear model with additive noise):
# X_0 = Normal distribution mu=0, sigma=1
# X_1 = 2 * X_0 + noise
# X_2 = 0.5 * X_1 + noise

graph = nx.DiGraph([('A', 'B'), ('B', 'C')])
column_mapping = {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 2}

rng = default_rng(0)
X_raw = np.zeros((500, 3))
X_raw[:, 0] = rng.normal(size=500)
X_raw[:, 1] = 2.0 * X_raw[:, 0] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500)
X_raw[:, 2] = 0.5 * X_raw[:, 1] + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=500)

scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
for node in graph.nodes:
    if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
        scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
    else:
        scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
            prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))

dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm, column_mapping).fit(X_raw)

# sample fresh data from the fitted DGP (signature: sample(rng, n))
Xs = dgp.sample(default_rng(1), 10)
print('sampled shape:', Xs.shape)

# intervene in place: pass a copy, fix the values in B (all = 10), recompute C downstream
Xi = dgp.intervene(X_raw.copy(), ['B'], [np.full(500, 10.0)], rng=default_rng(2))
print('B pinned:', np.allclose(Xi[:, 1], 10.0))
print('C propagated (B=10 -> C~5):', np.allclose(Xi[:, 2], 5.0, atol=0.5))

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Understand the building blocks — generators, selectors, DGPs, and pipelines — before going through the per-deficit tutorials.

docs.title: 1. Where generators live: the module structure¶
docs.text: Generators are grouped first by modality (tabular_data, time_series, text, image, graph, geolocated_data), then by deficit family (outliers, noise, drift, missingness, imbalance). Every family is a Python package of modules, and every generator is a class whose name ends in Generator.

docs.title: 2. Instantiate a generator¶
docs.text:
A generator is a plain Python class. Each generator takes a numpy.random.Generator at construction:

gen = SomeGenerator(random_generator=default_rng(seed))

docs.title: Adding rows, exemplified: outliers¶
docs.text: This example adds 10 outliers to X. Note what happens to the shape: the outliers are appended as new rows, so Xt is bigger than X.

docs.title: Deficit labels¶
docs.text: Some generators save which rows have been modified and expose this information through a dedicated getter — for outliers, get_outliers_labels():

docs.title: 4. Shape rules: what happens to Xt¶
docs.text:
The shape of Xt depends on the deficit family — there are exactly three modes:

Mode Effect on shape Adding rows Xt is larger than X (deficit rows appended) Changing values Xt has the same shape as X (existing values are changed) Removing rows Xt is smaller than X (affected rows are dropped)

docs.title: Changing values, exemplified: noise¶
docs.text: Additive noise replaces the existing values in place, so 100 rows stay 100 rows:

docs.title: Removing rows, exemplified: imbalance¶
docs.text: An imbalance generator removes the rows affected by the deficit. The only thing it needs to know is which rows — that decision is packaged in a selector (a boolean mask per column). Selectors are their own concept and get a full section below (section 5); here we just use one preset so the shape rule is visible: about half of the 100 rows are removed.

docs.title: 5. Selectors: which rows get the deficit¶
docs.text: Generators (drift, missingness, noise, imbalance, ...) accept a selector: an object that decides which rows receive the deficit.

docs.title: The contract¶
docs.text:
Selectors are index-only: they work on column positions, never on variable names (no column_mapping in the selector layer).

values = selector(X)   # -> dict[int, spec]

The dict keys are the column positions the deficit applies to. Per target column the spec is either:

  • a boolean mask — True = the deficit is applied to that row (deterministic), or
  • a float in [0, 1] (scalar = one level for the whole column) or a (n,) array — the probability that the deficit is applied to that row (1.0 = definitely, 0.0 = never).

The presets are self-contained: the positions they cover (columns) and the positions they read (class_column, column, driver) are all bound at construction as bare ints. Causal generators pass their targets positionally: the selector's columns ARE the intervention targets.

docs.text: Badgers ships selectors (see badgers.core.selectors):

docs.title: 6. Data-generating processes (DGP) and structural causal models (SCM)¶
docs.text:
Some generators use a structural causal model (SCM) to represent the underlying data-generating process (DGP). An SCM encodes how the columns come about, not just what they look like: each column is generated from its causal parents plus noise, following the edges of a causal graph. In badgers a DGP is an object that bundles:

  • a networkx.DiGraph describing the causal structure (an edge A -> B means A is a cause of B),
  • a column_mapping from node names to column positions in X, and
  • per-node causal mechanisms estimated from the data (e.g., a linear regression of the child on its parents plus a noise term).

This is what makes causal generators different from plain value edits: they intervene on a node (fix its values, do(B = v)), then sample — i.e. recompute that node's children and all their descendants from the SCM, so the whole downstream part of the data stays consistent with the causal structure.

docs.title: Functions:¶
docs.text:
dgp = GcmSCMDGP(scm).fit(X)                  # fit mechanisms (scm: a dowhy-gcm StructuralCausalModel)
Xs = dgp.sample(rng, n)                      # sample fresh data from the SCM
Xi = dgp.intervene(X.copy(), ['B'], [values], rng=rng)  # do(B = ...), descendants recomputed

docs.title: Backends:¶
docs.text: The shipped backends are two SCM adapters in badgers.core.dgp.backends: GcmSCMDGP wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel (extra badgers[dowhy]) and PyMCSCMDGP wraps a PyMC pm.Model (extra badgers[pymc]) — build the SCM with the wrapped library's own API, then hand it over. There is no default backend: causal generators require an explicit dgp=. See the dev notebook Using DGPs for the two adapters in action.

docs.title: 7. Pipelines: chaining deficits¶
docs.text: Deficits compose. A Pipeline takes a dict of generators (the keys are step names) and applies them in order, passing each output to the next step. Per-step parameters are passed at generate() time keyed by the step name:

docs.text: Two generators built from the same seed produce bit-identical results — the reproducibility contract in action:

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Generators are instantiated with an rng and called via generate(X, **params) — they take X only and return the single generated object Xt; target-like data lives in dedicated columns of X.
  • Shape rules: appending (outliers), shape-preserving (noise, missingness), row-changing (imbalance: removing or duplicating rows).
  • Selectors decide which rows are affected; DGPs model the data-generating process; pipelines compose generators.

def _plot_selector_scores(selectors, X, title):
    """One panel per selector over X; bool masks drawn red/green,
    float scores with a red-to-green colormap. The first axis shows
    the f0 reference column."""
    n_sel = len(selectors)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n_sel + 1, figsize=(3.2 * (n_sel + 1), 3.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    f0 = X[:, 0]
    order = np.argsort(f0)
    axes[0].scatter(f0[order], np.arange(len(order)), c=f0[order], cmap='viridis', s=15)
    axes[0].set_title('f0 (sorted)')
    axes[0].set_xlabel('f0 value')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('row index')
    for ax, (name, sel) in zip(axes[1:], selectors):
        out = sel(X)
        if isinstance(out, dict):
            specs = [np.asarray(s, dtype=float) for s in out.values()]
            scores = np.broadcast_to(specs[0], (len(X),)) if specs[0].ndim == 0 else specs[0]
        else:
            scores = np.asarray(out, dtype=float)
        if scores.dtype == bool:
            colors = np.where(scores, 'C3', 'C2')
            ax.scatter(f0, np.arange(len(f0)), c=colors, s=15)
        else:
            # selection specs (float scalar or (n,) array) collapse a scalar
            # onto the 0..1 scale — scale per selector so the gradient is visible
            hi = scores.max()
            sc = ax.scatter(f0, np.arange(len(f0)), c=scores, cmap='RdYlGn_r', vmin=0, vmax=hi, s=15)
            fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, shrink=0.8, label=f'score (max {hi:.3f})')
        ax.set_title(name)
        ax.set_xlabel('f0 value')
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig

class ThresholdSelector:
    """Select rows whose reference column exceeds a fixed threshold.

    Returns a BOOLEAN mask (deterministic case of the contract).
    """

    def __init__(self, columns, column, threshold=0.0):
        self.columns = tuple(columns)
        self.column = int(column)
        self.threshold = threshold

    def __call__(self, X, targets=None):
        targets = self.columns if targets is None else tuple(targets)
        extra = [c for c in targets if c not in self.columns]
        if extra:
            raise ValueError(f"targets {extra} outside the selector's columns {self.columns}")
        col = X[:, self.column]
        return {c: col > self.threshold for c in targets}

    def __repr__(self):
        return (f"ThresholdSelector(columns={self.columns!r}, "
                f"column={self.column}, threshold={self.threshold})")

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))


class SmoothThresholdSelector:
    """Scores: P(deficit) = sigmoid((col - threshold) / slope)."""

    def __init__(self, columns, column, threshold=0.0, slope=1.0):
        self.columns = tuple(columns)
        self.column = int(column)
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.slope = slope

    def __call__(self, X, targets=None):
        targets = self.columns if targets is None else tuple(targets)
        extra = [c for c in targets if c not in self.columns]
        if extra:
            raise ValueError(f"targets {extra} outside the selector's columns {self.columns}")
        col = X[:, self.column]
        scores = sigmoid((col - self.threshold) / self.slope)
        assert np.all((scores >= 0) & (scores <= 1))
        return {c: scores for c in targets}

docs.title: Creating selectors¶
docs.text:
This notebook explains the selector contract in full detail and shows how to implement, validate and consume a custom selector.

Selectors are the objects that decide which rows of the data receive a deficit (outlier / missing value / noise / drift / drop). A generator that accepts a selector delegates the who to the selector and keeps the what to itself.

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Write a custom selector: the index-only selection-spec contract (which rows a deficit is applied to, keyed by column position), the preset implementations, and how generators turn the specs into deficits.

docs.title: The contract¶
docs.text:
A selector is any callable with the signature:

selector(X, targets=None) -> dict[int, spec]

The dict keys are column positions (ints) of X — the columns the deficit applies to; there is no column_mapping and no variable-name lookup in the selector layer. Per target column, the returned spec is one of:

  • a boolean mask (True = deficit applied to that row) — the value-free presets return selection decisions;
    • AlwaysSelector returns the constant scalar spec 1.0 per target (realizes to all-true) — BernoulliSelector and ExactCountSelector return boolean masks — and value-driven presets return [0, 1] selection specs;
  • a float in [0, 1] (a scalar = one level for the whole column) or a (n,) float array — the probability that the deficit is applied to that row (1.0 = definitely, 0.0 = never). A (n,) bool array is also a valid spec; a plain bool scalar is NOT (it is ambiguous — use a mask).

The presets are self-contained: their columns (the positions they cover, and the default call-time targets) and the column(s) they READ (e.g. class_column, column, driver) are all bound at construction as bare int positions. Nothing is passed at call time — so an intensity sweep means constructing a new selector.

Exception: a caller may pass targets explicitly at call time — selector(X, targets=[...]). Causal generators no longer take call-time target arguments: the selector's columns (integer column positions) ARE their intervention targets.

docs.title: How generators turn specs into deficits¶
docs.text:
A spec only says how likely each row is to be affected — it does not apply anything. Realizing it is the consuming generator's job, and there is a single rule for every deficit type:

selected = rng.random(n) < np.broadcast_to(spec, (n,))   # Bernoulli selection

(shape-preserving generators: noise, drift, missingness — every row keeps its place; a row with spec 0.3 is affected in 30% of the draws). The helper get_selected_fields(X, selector, rng) implements exactly this: it returns the narrow boolean selection field of shape (n_rows, n_targets) where column i belongs to the selector's i-th target, each column realized with the single rule rng.random(n) < spec; row-level union is get_selected_fields(X, selector, rng).any(axis=1).

Row-removing generators (the imbalance UndersamplingGenerator) use the same realization to mark the rows that are dropped: a boolean spec drops exactly its selected rows, and a fractional spec drops each row stochastically with probability equal to the spec — so high-score rows disappear more often.

docs.title: Comparing the bundled selectors¶
docs.text:
All three bundled selectors below act on the same single column, position 0 of X. The helper _plot_selector_scores draws one panel per selector so they can be compared side by side on the same rows: the first axis shows column 0 (sorted) as a reference for the row order, the next three are the selectors applied to those rows.

Selector Spec type What the panel shows AlwaysSelector([0]) constant scalar spec 1.0[^note-always] every row affected BernoulliSelector([0], rate=0.3) bool mask a random ~30% of rows ProportionalSelector([0], column=0) float spec deficit probability rising with column 0

[^note-always]: value-free preset: the constant scalar spec 1.0 realizes to all-true, so every row is affected.

Bool masks draw red for affected rows, green for untouched ones; float specs use a red-to-green colormap (red = high deficit probability). Note the constructor order: every preset takes the column positions it covers first, the positions it reads (column=) after.

docs.title: Building a custom selector¶
docs.text: The minimal recipe ? a class with __call__(self, X, targets=None) returning a {column_position: spec} dict. We build a threshold selector: select rows whose reference column (an int position bound at construction) exceeds a constructor-time threshold.

docs.title: A score-returning variant¶
docs.text: Now the probabilistic flavor: instead of a mask we return the probability that each row is affected. We make it a smooth function of the reference column ? the further above the threshold, the closer to 1.0. Notice the selector draws no randomness.

docs.title: Consuming the selector with a real generator¶
docs.text:
Selectors are only useful through generators.

Below we use our SmoothThresholdSelector (float specs) with the UndersamplingGenerator and verify that the rows that survive skew toward low-score rows (the high-score rows are the ones dropped).

docs.title: Conformance checklist¶
docs.text:
Before contributing a selector, check:

  • constructor binds columns as int positions and every read column (column, class_column, driver, ...) as a bare int, and raises clearly on anything else;
  • __call__ accepts (X, targets=None) and validates call-time targets against the constructor columns;
  • returned dict keys are exactly the resolved target positions;
  • specs are bool masks or floats/(n,) arrays in [0, 1] ? never a plain bool scalar (assert internally);

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• A selector returns dict[int, spec]: keys are column positions; specs are bool masks (decisions) or floats in [0, 1] (deficit probabilities) ? never a bool scalar.
  • Selectors never draw randomness for their rates; the consuming generator realizes every spec with the single rule rng.random(n) < spec.
  • Presets are self-contained: constructor columns + read columns are int positions; an intensity sweep means constructing a new selector.

class MyGenerator(GeneratorMixin):
    """
    Flip a fraction of class labels to another class.

    The class labels are expected to live INSIDE X, in a dedicated
    column (`class_column`). Which rows get flipped is decided by a
    Selector
    (badgers.core.selectors): the selector draws the flag, the
    generator only realizes the defect.
    """

    def __init__(self, random_generator: np.random.Generator):
        """
        :param random_generator: A random gen
        """
        self.random_generator = random_generator

    @preprocess_inputs
    def generate(self, X, *, class_column: int = -1, selector=None):
        """
        Flip a fraction of the labels (column `class_column` of X) to a
        different class.
        :param X: features, with the class labels in column `class_column`
        :param class_column: column of X holding the class labels
        :param selector: a Selector deciding which rows are selected; defaults to
            BernoulliSelector over the label column, bound to the
            generator rng (position 1 = the `class` column of the demo
            data above)
        """
        if selector is None:
            # selectors take positions: resolve the (possibly negative)
            # class_column into a column position
            col = class_column if class_column >= 0 else X.shape[1] + class_column
            selector = BernoulliSelector([col], rate=0.1,
                                         rng=self.random_generator)
        # the selector draws the flag: one iid Bernoulli per row
        flag = next(iter(selector(X).values()))
        # each flagged row gets a new label: any class except its own
        labels = X[:, class_column]
        classes = np.unique(labels)
        Xt = X.copy()
        flag_idx = np.flatnonzero(flag)
        if flag_idx.size:
            # vectorized "different class" choice: draw uniformly, shift
            # the rows that drew their own class to the next class
            k = classes.size
            own = np.searchsorted(classes, labels[flag_idx])
            choice = self.random_generator.integers(0, k, size=flag_idx.size)
            choice = np.where(choice == own, (choice + 1) % k, choice)
            Xt[flag_idx, class_column] = classes[choice]
        return Xt

class MyGenerator(GeneratorMixin):
    """
    Flip a fraction of class labels to another class
    (a realistic name would be ClassFlipGenerator)
    """

    def __init__(self, random_generator: np.random.Generator):
        """
        :param random_generator: A random gen
        """
        self.random_generator = random_generator

    @preprocess_inputs
    def generate(self, X, *, class_column: int = -1,
                 flip_rate: float = 0.1, selector=None):
        """
        Flip `flip_rate` of the labels to a different class.
        :param X: features, with the class labels in column `class_column`
        :param class_column: column of X holding the class labels
        :param flip_rate: fraction of rows whose label is flipped
            (used to build the default BernoulliSelector)
        :param selector: a Selector taking over row selection when given
        """
        if selector is None:
            # selectors take positions: resolve the (possibly negative)
            # class_column into a column position
            col = class_column if class_column >= 0 else X.shape[1] + class_column
            selector = BernoulliSelector([col], rate=flip_rate,
                                         rng=self.random_generator)
        flag = next(iter(selector(X).values()))
        labels = X[:, class_column]
        classes = np.unique(labels)
        Xt = X.copy()
        flag_idx = np.flatnonzero(flag)
        if flag_idx.size:
            k = classes.size
            own = np.searchsorted(classes, labels[flag_idx])
            choice = self.random_generator.integers(0, k, size=flag_idx.size)
            choice = np.where(choice == own, (choice + 1) % k, choice)
            Xt[flag_idx, class_column] = classes[choice]
        return Xt

class DGPGenerator(GeneratorMixin):
    """Push the given rows off their fitted mechanism by
    intervening through a DGP object: fresh noise for the
    perturbation nodes, descendants recomputed through the
    fitted mechanisms."""

    def __init__(self, random_generator: np.random.Generator,
                 dgp=None):
        """
        :param random_generator: the rng, as for any generator
        :param dgp: a fitted DGP object (structure: given at
            construction, like the rng)
        """
        self.random_generator = random_generator
        self.dgp = dgp

    @preprocess_inputs
    def generate(self, X, **params):
        """
        :param selector: the selector whose columns own the intervention
            targets (its selected rows are pushed off mechanism)
        :param n_outliers: number of rows to push off mechanism
        """
        selector = params['selector']
        n_outliers = params['n_outliers']
        # the selector owns the targets: select cells, then pick selected rows
        selected = get_selected_fields(X, selector, self.random_generator).any(axis=1)
        # pick the selected rows to disturb, then let the DGP do the work:
        # fresh rows sampled through the fitted mechanisms
        row_idx = self.random_generator.choice(np.flatnonzero(selected),
                                               size=n_outliers, replace=False)
        Xt = X.copy()
        Xt[row_idx] = self.dgp.sample(self.random_generator, n_outliers)
        return Xt

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Write a new tabular generator step by step: the GeneratorMixin contract, generate signatures, testing, and benchmark registration.

docs.title: Creating a (tabular_data) generator: Scenario¶
docs.text:
Label noise is a common data-quality defect: some rows carry the wrong class label, and classifiers trained on such data silently degrade.

The generator here flips a fraction of the class labels to another class: for a row picked at random with probability flip_rate, the label is replaced by a different class.

docs.title: Create the generator class¶
docs.text: Every generator inherits from GeneratorMixin (so the import comes first). This enforces implementing a generate(X, **params) function.

docs.title: Add a random generator¶
docs.text:
That is just best practice so that we can seed the random number generator and reproduce the generation

We add it to the constructor code, give it a type hint (it should be a numpy.random.Generator object) and the type hint should be a numpy.random.Generator object; it is required (no default) -- the user of your generator must pass one

docs.title: Add the preprocess_inputs decorator¶
docs.text:
As a convention for tabular data generators, X is expected to be a numpy array. Note that badgers implements a utility to preprocess inputs such as lists, list of lists, pandas DataFrames and convert them to numpy arrays. So that a user can actually input other data types than just numpy arrays. This utility comes in the form of a decorator and is called preprocess_inputs.

from badgers.core.decorators.tabular_data import preprocess_inputs

The decorator wraps a generate(self, X, **params) method: it takes X only; the class labels live in a dedicated column of X.

docs.title: Add the code to transform/generate the data.¶
docs.text:
The algorithm goes like this:

  • the class labels live INSIDE X, in a dedicated column (class_column).
  • WHICH rows get flipped is decided by a Selector (next section).
  • each flagged row gets a new label: a class chosen at random among the classes that are NOT its current label.

X keeps its shape (a copy — generators never mutate their input); only the label column changes, and generate returns that single transformed array.

docs.title: Add a Selector for the flagged rows¶
docs.text:
WHICH rows get flipped is decided by a Selector (badgers.core.selectors), not by hand-rolled code like flag = self.random_generator.random(n) < rate inside generate.

A Selector is a callable returning dict[int, spec]: the keys are column positions, the specs are boolean masks (or probability scores in [0, 1]) per row. The presets draw with the generator's own rng (a single rng stream), so the selection is reproducible together with the rest of the generation:

  • BernoulliSelector(columns, rate, rng) — one iid Bernoulli flag per row with probability rate (completely at random);
  • AlwaysSelector(columns) — every row is selected;
  • TopQuantileSelector / ClassSelector / ... — value- or class-based rules.

Separating the row-selection rule (the selector) from the defect itself (the flip) is the pattern the shipped generators follow: the same selector presets gate any defect form (missing values, noise, outliers, ...).

docs.title: Let's try it¶
docs.text:
First, we generate some data using sklearn make_blob utility.

Second, we instantiate our generator and apply the generate function on our data.

Finally, we plot the data using matplotlib.

docs.title: Create some fake data and plot it¶
Plot the initial and the transformed data¶
Let's add some parameters¶
docs.text: Generators take their parameters as arguments of generate (or at construction). The selection rule is a Selector: the generator builds its default BernoulliSelector([1], rate=flip_rate) from the flip_rate parameter — or a caller-provided selector takes over.

docs.title: Instantiate the generator, generate data with different flip_rate values and plot the result¶
docs.text: Higher flip_rate means more shuffled colors in the transformed panels — the cluster shapes never move, only the label colors do.

docs.title: A generator that uses an existing DGP¶
docs.text:
A generator does not have to invent its own mechanism: it can reuse a fitted DGP object and wrap its sampling or do- machinery into the generate contract. Build the SCM with the library of choice (dowhy-gcm or PyMC) and wrap it with an adapter — GcmSCMDGP (extra pip install badgers[dowhy]) or PyMCSCMDGP (extra pip install badgers[pymc]); see Using-DGPs.ipynb for the functionality showcase and the Creating DGP notebooks for building custom ones.

Here the generator keeps ONE thing in its constructor — the DGP object (this is structure, exactly like the rng) — and passes everything else (selector, n_outliers) to generate.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• A generator that reuses a DGP stores the DGP object in its constructor (structure, like the rng) and scenario parameters in generate.
  • Build the SCM with the wrapped library's own API and wrap it with GcmSCMDGP/PyMCSCMDGP — there is no default backend.
  • The do-machinery (severing edges, recomputing descendants) comes from the DGP; the generator only picks rows and passes them through.

docs.title: Final notes:¶
docs.text:
In badgers all generators are organized first by type of modality (tabular_data, time_series, text, etc.) and by type of data quality problem (noise, outliers, drift, etc.): for instance badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise, badgers.generators.time_series.noise, etc.

By convention, one parent class groups all generators that "belong together".

For instance in badgers.generators.tabular_data.noise there is a NoiseGenerator class that serves as parent for the other generators, for instance GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator and AdditiveNoiseGenerator.

This is sometimes useful to do so. For example for storing intern attributes that all generators of this family will need (that is the case in missing values, or in patterns generation).

Some parameters (like flip_rate in our example) will be more specific and might be called at "generation" time (i.e., once we call generate(X, **params)). The advantage is that one creates only one object and can call the generate function with different parameters.

Which parameters need to be given at construction time and at generation time depends on the use case. In general: keep the minimum in the constructor (a random generator, and objects that define the structure) and pass the scenario parameters to the generate call.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Subclass GeneratorMixin (or the tabular base class) and implement generate.
  • Instantiate with an rng; never rely on global numpy randomness.
  • Register the generator in the benchmark framework to measure its cost.

import pymc as pm

# 1. write the SCM as a PyMC model: structural nodes observed,
#    free RVs are the unknown parameters, functions go in the params
with pm.Model() as scm_pm:
    mu_A = pm.Normal('mu_A', 0, 2)
    sigma_A = pm.HalfNormal('sigma_A', 1)
    A = pm.Normal('A', mu=mu_A, sigma=sigma_A, observed=X[:, 0])
    sigma_B = pm.HalfNormal('sigma_B', 1)
    B = pm.Normal('B', mu=pm.math.sin(A), sigma=sigma_B, observed=X[:, 1])
    beta_C = pm.Normal('beta_C', 0, 2)
    sigma_C = pm.HalfNormal('sigma_C', 1)
    C = pm.Normal('C', mu=beta_C * B, sigma=sigma_C, observed=X[:, 2])

# 2. hand it to badgers — one joint MCMC run, full posterior kept
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import PyMCSCMDGP

pm_scm_dgp = PyMCSCMDGP(scm_pm, column_mapping, n_draws=200).fit(X)

docs.title: Using DGPs¶
docs.text:
A DGP (badgers.core.dgp) carries the causal graph plus one fitted mechanism per node and exposes fit/sample/intervene. The only shipped backends are two adapters that wrap externally built structural causal models:

Backend Extra Wraps Documentation GcmSCMDGP badgers[dowhy] a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel dowhy.gcm PyMCSCMDGP badgers[pymc] a PyMC pm.Model (structural nodes observed) pymc

docs.title: Fit and sample¶
docs.text:
• Here we first create a synthetic dataset from a simple SCM (a chain A ->- B- > C) where the effects are linear.
  • We model the SCM using dohy.gcm (also using linear effects)

docs.title: Interventions: the do-operator¶
docs.text: intervene(rows, nodes, values) pins the given nodes, re-samples their non-descendants' noise, and recomputes descendants through the fitted mechanisms — causal surgery, not just column edits.

docs.title: Plugging a DGP into a causal generator¶
docs.text:
Any DGP works with every causal generator. The generator performs the intervention itself (severing incoming edges of the perturbation nodes, fresh noise for ancestors, recomputing descendants through the DGP).

In this example we inject outliers values in node A and these values propagate through the SCM to B and C.

docs.title: Building the SCM externally: dowhy-gcm¶
docs.text: GcmSCMDGP wraps a dowhy-gcm StructuralCausalModel built outside badgers: assign a mechanism per node with dowhy-gcm's own API, then hand the whole model over. badgers runs the graph and exposes fit/sample/intervene — dowhy-gcm stays the home of the mechanism definitions.

docs.title: Building the SCM externally: PyMC¶
docs.text: PyMCSCMDGP wraps a user-written pm.Model: the structural nodes are observed RVs named in column_mapping, and the structural functions live in the distribution parameters (here sin(A) in the mean of B). One joint pm.sample keeps the full posterior — every cascade pins ONE coherent draw, same seed, same draw.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• One protocol: fit(X), then sample(rng, n) and intervene(rows, nodes, values, rng=...) — identical across backends.
  • GcmSCMDGP uses a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel
  • PyMCSCMDGP uses a pm.Model

from badgers.generators.tabular_data.drift.causal import CausalDriftGenerator


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

docs.title: Generating drift¶
docs.text:
Drift is a systematic shift of the data distribution: the same data-generating process starts producing values that are translated (or scaled) compared to the values observed before.

This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers to inject drift, in increasing complexity:

  1. Acting on the observation process — directly translate the observed values of one or several columns (this can represent a change in the measurement process, a systematic bias in a sensor, etc.). No causal model is involved; these generators do not use a DGP and do not propagate anything: the change is exactly the shift requested. badgers offers them in two flavors:
    • deterministic (FixedShiftGenerator, FixedShiftClassesGenerator): every affected value is translated by exactly the requested amount, in a fully reproducible way;
    • random (RandomShiftGenerator, RandomShiftClassesGenerator): the shift magnitude is drawn from a normal distribution whose standard deviation is the requested amount.
  2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — perturb a node of a fitted causal model and let the shift propagate to the descendants through the structural equations (CausalDriftGenerator).

All of them accept a selector to decide which rows are affected (see the Understanding badgers notebook for the selector contract).

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Translate the data distribution: deterministic fixed shifts first, then random shifts with signed per-column magnitudes, then per-class drift on a causal graph.

docs.title: Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶
docs.text: What these generators do: they standardize X (each column to mean 0, variance 1), add the shift, and un-standardize. The result is a translation of the observed values only — no causal structure is used, and nothing propagates beyond the shifted columns.

docs.title: Deterministic: translate all rows (FixedShiftGenerator)¶
docs.text: Every value of the selected columns is translated by exactly shift standard deviations (the parameter may be a scalar or a signed per-column array). No random number is drawn, so the same input always produces the same output — useful for controlled, reproducible benchmark scenarios.

docs.title: Deterministic: translate per class (FixedShiftClassesGenerator)¶
docs.text:
The class values are read from a column of X (here the last column, cls, position 2). A ClassSelector builds one boolean mask per class value: each class gets its own shift — here given as a dict {class_value: shift}. Every class value present among the selected rows must have an entry (a missing one raises ValueError); plain-int keys work for a float-encoded class column (keys are normalized against its dtype).

Note: the class column is never shifted (it defines which rows are affected, so modifying it would corrupt the selection). The class column is read from the selector's class_column — the selector owns the class information. Pass variables= to restrict/override the columns that get shifted.

docs.title: Random: translate all rows (RandomShiftGenerator)¶
docs.text: Same contract as the deterministic version, but the shift actually applied is drawn from a normal distribution: for each column the draw is N(0, shift_std) * sign(shift_std) — the absolute value of shift_std sets the scale, its sign sets the direction. With a scalar shift_std all columns get independent draws of the same scale.

docs.title: Random: translate per class (RandomShiftClassesGenerator)¶
docs.text: Each class gets its own independent shift draw. shift_std may be a scalar (same scale for every class) or a dict {class_value: std}.

docs.title: What shift / shift_std / shift_amount actually mean¶
docs.text:
Both parameters express the shift in units of the column's standard deviation (sigma). Internally every drift generator does:

z = (X - mean) / std          # normalize: each column has sigma = 1
z += shift                    # deterministic (FixedShift*): the parameter IS the shift
                              # random: shift ~ N(0, shift_std * sigma)
X' = z * std + mean           # un-normalize

So shift = 2 / shift_std = 2 on column f0 means exactly: "move column f0 by 2 of its own standard deviations" — a column with a wide range gets a proportionally larger absolute shift than a narrow one. The shift is a single value per column, applied to all affected rows (that is what makes it drift and not noise — noise redraws per row). The deterministic generators apply it verbatim; the random ones draw it once.

docs.title: Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶
docs.text: What the generator does: CausalDriftGenerator takes a fitted DGP (a causal model of the data). It shifts a node of choice, then re-evaluates the structural equations of the descendants on the shifted rows (Pearl surgery): the change propagates exactly as it would in the real system. Only downstream nodes are affected; upstream nodes and untouched rows stay as they were.

docs.title: 1. Build the causal graph¶
docs.text: We use a three-node chain X -> Y -> Z. The node names are symbolic; a column_mapping maps them to column positions of X.

docs.title: 2. Generate data from the DAG¶
docs.text: Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

docs.title: 3. Fit the DGP¶
docs.text: The GcmSCMDGP adapter wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel: every non-root node's mechanism is a linear AdditiveNoiseModel fitted on the original data, root nodes resample the observed values. The SCM is built with dowhy-gcm's own API (see the make_scm helper).

docs.title: 4. Generate causally-propagated drift¶
docs.text: We shift node Y and watch it propagate to Z (but not to X).

docs.title: Propagation to the descendant (Y → Z)¶
docs.text: The drift is a single systematic shift, but the propagation is Pearl surgery with fresh noise: Z is not translated by a rigid delta — it is recomputed from its (shifted) parent through the fitted structural equation, Z_new = f(Y_shifted) + fresh_noise. The systematic part of the shift carries through (Z moves because Y moved), but Z's scatter is re-rolled, not preserved: the descendant cloud keeps roughly its original width while its position follows the parent's shift. This is what distinguishes drift from noise: drift shifts a node systematically (one draw applied to all affected rows), noise scatters it row-by-row — and in both cases the descendants' noise is freshly drawn, never inherited.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Lever Generator Uses a DGP? Propagates? Deterministic? Selector support observation process FixedShiftGenerator no no (values only) yes — observation process, per class FixedShiftClassesGenerator no no (values only) yes ClassSelector observation process RandomShiftGenerator no no (values only) no — observation process, per class RandomShiftClassesGenerator no no (values only) no ClassSelector DGP CausalDriftGenerator yes (fitted) yes — descendants re-evaluated no yes (boolean masks)
  • Drift is a single systematic shift per column, applied to all affected rows — in contrast to noise, which redraws per row.
  • shift_std / shift_amount / shift are in units of the column's standard deviation (normalize, shift, un-normalize).
  • The class column is never shifted by the per-class generators (it defines the selection); it is read from the selector's class_column — the selector owns the class information. Use variables= (int positions) to make the shifted columns explicit.
  • Generators mutate X in place — pass X.copy() to keep the original.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Drift translates columns in units of their standard deviation (data are standardized first).
  • FixedShiftGenerator is deterministic (same input, same output); RandomShiftGenerator draws one shift per column with a signed magnitude.
  • Per-class drift (RandomShiftClassesGenerator) never shifts the class column itself.

docs.title: Generating class imbalance¶
docs.text:
Imbalance is a row-changing deficit: instead of (or in addition to) changing values, the generator removes or duplicates rows — so Xt is smaller than X (undersampling) or a superset of X (oversampling; no row is ever dropped). Real datasets are rarely balanced: rare events, censored observations, or biased sampling processes skew the row distribution. This makes pipelines that assume balanced classes or uniform feature coverage fail in instructive ways.

This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

  1. UndersamplingGenerator — removes the rows flagged by a deficit selector (ClassSelector for exact per-class drops, ProportionalSelector for score-driven stochastic removal).
  2. OversamplingGenerator — duplicates rows according to a per-row multiplicity selector (ConstantMultiplicity for uniform copies, MaskedMultiplicity for copies of selected rows only).

Both generators act on the observation process only — they do not use a DGP: rows are removed or copied as-is, so any relationships between columns are preserved on the surviving/duplicated rows.

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Remove rows so that some classes (or score regions) become under-represented, or duplicate rows so that some classes become over-represented — imbalance applied with selectors.

docs.title: Sample data from different classes¶
docs.text: What the selector does here: ClassSelector([0, 1], class_column=2, ...) reads the class labels from position 2 and builds one boolean mask per class value from the given shares. The shares are fractions of the total row count, clipped to the rows available in each class; classes absent from proportions are kept as-is. UndersamplingGenerator then removes exactly the affected rows.

docs.title: Sample data proportionally to a column (stochastic removal)¶
docs.text:
What the selector does here: ProportionalSelector([0, 1], column=0) reads column 0 (f0) and returns per-row float scores in [0, 1] — the deficit probability grows with the value of f0. The consumer, UndersamplingGenerator, removes each row stochastically with probability equal to its deficit score: rows with a HIGH deficit probability are dropped often, rows with a LOW one are kept most of the time. The result concentrates on small-f0 rows — a form of imbalance driven by a continuous column.

For illustration we also compute a demo ranking variable score and use it as a color: it is not a target and plays no role in the selection.

docs.title: Part B — Oversampling (duplicating rows)¶
docs.text:
The mirror image of undersampling: instead of dropping rows, the OversamplingGenerator duplicates them according to a per-row integer multiplicity (1 = keep the row as-is, k > 1 = keep k copies). Two invariants:

  • the output is a superset of the input — no row is ever dropped, and the original row order is preserved;
  • get_imbalance_labels() reports, for each input row, whether it was duplicated (True = multiplicity > 1).

Multiplicity selectors: ConstantMultiplicity(k) assigns every row k copies; MaskedMultiplicity(mask, k) assigns k copies to the rows where mask is True (a (n,) bool array or a callable on X) and 1 to the rest. Multiplicities must be integers >= 1 — fractional values are rejected (they look like a deficit Selector; use UndersamplingGenerator for that).

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Generator Effect on shape Selection parameter UndersamplingGenerator removes rows per deficit selector deficit Selector: ClassSelector (per-class shares), ProportionalSelector (float scores), boolean masks OversamplingGenerator duplicates rows per per-row multiplicity ConstantMultiplicity(k), MaskedMultiplicity(mask, k), or an (n,) int array of multiplicities (all >= 1)
  • Imbalance is a row-changing deficit: undersampling makes Xt smaller than X, oversampling makes it a superset (no row dropped, order preserved).
  • The selector decides who is affected; the generator realizes the decision.
  • Both generators are observation-process operations — no DGP is involved, so the surviving/duplicated rows stay structurally consistent by construction.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• UndersamplingGenerator removes the rows flagged by a deficit selector; OversamplingGenerator duplicates rows per per-row multiplicity.
  • Selectors quantify which rows are affected; intensities (rate, quantile, multiplicity, mask) are constructor arguments.
  • Neither generator uses a DGP: rows are removed or copied as-is, so any relationships between columns are preserved on the output rows.
  • get_imbalance_labels() aligns with the input rows: True = removed (undersampling) or duplicated (oversampling).

docs.text:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from numpy.random import default_rng
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

from badgers.generators.tabular_data.missingness import (
    MissingCompletelyAtRandom, DummyMissingAtRandom, DummyMissingNotAtRandom,
)
from badgers.generators.tabular_data.missingness.causal import CausalMissingnessGenerator
import dowhy.gcm as gcm
from badgers.core.dgp.backends import GcmSCMDGP
from badgers.core.selectors import BernoulliSelector, TopQuantileSelector

rng = default_rng(seed=0)


def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(

docs.title: Generating missing data¶
docs.text:
Missingness is the defect where some observed values are simply not recorded (np.nan in the output). Real pipelines rarely get to see complete data: sensors drop out, forms are left blank, values exceed a recording range. The mechanism matters as much as the amount — the same 20% of missing values behaves very differently depending on why the values are missing:

Mechanism Meaning In badgers (selector) Legacy one-parameter MCAR — missing completely at random a value goes missing independently of everything else BernoulliSelector([col], rate=...) MissingCompletelyAtRandom MAR — missing at random missingness depends on another, observed variable (e.g. values of X are high) TopQuantileSelector([col], column=..., driver=...) DummyMissingAtRandom MNAR — missing not at random a value's own (unobserved) magnitude drives its missingness TopQuantileSelector on itself DummyMissingNotAtRandom

The notebook shows both ways of expressing these mechanisms:

  1. Acting on the observation process — the legacy one-parameter generators: percentage_missing decides how much goes missing, the generator class decides why. They do not use a DGP and nothing is propagated.
  2. Explicit selectors — the same three mechanisms expressed as selector objects, which decide which cells are selected. Intensity (rate / quantile) lives on the selector, not on generate().

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Hide cells (write NaN) with different mechanisms: completely at random, related to another column (MAR), or related to the hidden value itself (MNAR) — including the causal-graph variant.

docs.title: Part A — Acting on the observation process (legacy one-parameter, no DGP)¶
docs.text: These generators take a single percentage_missing value: how much goes missing. Why it goes missing is hard-coded by the class (MCAR / MAR / MNAR). No causal model is involved and no propagation happens.

docs.title: Missing completely at random (MCAR)¶
docs.text: MissingCompletelyAtRandom replaces values with np.nan independently at random — the fact that a value is missing carries no information.

docs.title: Missing at random (MAR)¶
docs.text: DummyMissingAtRandom makes missingness depend on another, observed feature: for each column, a reference column is drawn uniformly at random among the other columns, and the missing probability grows as the (normalized, reversed) values of that reference column. Low values of the reference column go missing first. Looking only at observed data one can partly explain the missingness (it correlates with the reference column), but it cannot be fully predicted.

docs.title: Missing not at random (MNAR)¶
docs.text: DummyMissingNotAtRandom makes a value's own magnitude drive its missingness (unlike the other two generators, percentage_missing has no default value — pass it explicitly): the larger the original value, the more likely it is missing. Here the missingness biases the observed data — e.g. peak values systematically vanish.

docs.title: Part B — Explicit selectors on a causal graph¶
docs.text: CausalMissingnessGenerator expresses the same three mechanisms with selector objects on a fitted DGP. It writes NaN at the affected cells of the perturbation nodes and does not propagate: missingness is a property of the measurement process, not of the data-generating process (a descendant can still be observed).

docs.title: Build the graph, generate data, fit the DGP¶
MCAR: a value-blind selector¶
docs.text: BernoulliSelector([1], rate=...) — each row is affected independently with probability rate.

docs.title: MNAR: values drive their own missingness¶
docs.text: With the self-mode TopQuantileSelector, the largest values of Y itself are the ones that go missing (here the top 30%):

docs.title: MAR: a fully-observed reference column¶
docs.text: With reference-mode TopQuantileSelector, missingness of Y is driven by the observed value of X (the top half of X values):

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Lever Generator Uses a DGP? Propagates? Mechanism parameter observation process (legacy) MissingCompletelyAtRandom no no class = MCAR, percentage_missing = amount observation process (legacy) DummyMissingAtRandom no no class = MAR, percentage_missing = amount observation process (legacy) DummyMissingNotAtRandom no no class = MNAR, percentage_missing = amount selectors on a causal graph CausalMissingnessGenerator yes (fitted) no (observation layer) selector object = mechanism and intensity
  • With the selector version, intensity (rate / quantile) is configured on the selector, not on generate().
  • Missingness never cascades: it is a property of the measurement, not of the data-generating process.
  • Generators mutate X in place — pass X.copy() to keep the original.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Missingness only hides cells (NaN); values and shape are untouched.
  • The mechanism decides which cells hide: random (MCAR), conditioned on another column (MAR), or on the value itself (MNAR).
  • The causal variant is chooser-only: hidden cells do not cascade to descendants.

def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):

        else:

                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

docs.title: Generating noise¶
docs.text:
Noise is a row-wise perturbation of the observed values: each affected row gets its own random deviation, drawn independently (in contrast to drift, where one systematic shift is applied to all affected rows). Use noise to make a pipeline robust to measurement error, sensor jitter, or rounding — the signal is still there, but each observation is a bit off.

This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

  1. Acting on the observation process — add noise directly to the observed values (AdditiveNoiseGenerator, GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator). These generators do not use a DGP and nothing propagates: the value is changed exactly where the noise lands.
  2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — inject noise at a node of a fitted causal model and let it propagate to the descendants (CausalNoiseGenerator).

Both accept a selector to decide which rows are affected (see the Understanding badgers notebook for the selector contract).

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Corrupt values with additive noise: per-class white noise, noise drawn from any scipy distribution, and noise injected into a causal graph with descendants recomputed.

docs.title: Load and prepare data¶
docs.text: We first load an existing dataset from sklearn.datasets. The class values are stored as a column of X, so plotting uses the explicit vector cls.

docs.title: Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶
Add noise to all values¶
docs.text: AdditiveNoiseGenerator adds a draw from distribution to every cell of X — each row gets its own independent deviation.

docs.title: Add noise per class¶
docs.text:
GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator combines two independent parameters that are easy to confuse:

  • the selector decides which rows receive noise. It returns one boolean mask (or deficit probability) per class value. In the demo below, {0: 1., 1: 1., 2: 1., 3: 1.} means: every row of every class affected with probability 1 — so all rows are noisy. Set a value to 0.5 and half of that class's rows would be noisy (Bernoulli-wise); set it to 0. and that class stays clean.
  • noise_std_per_class decides how strong the noise is on the affected rows, per class: {0: 0.1, 1: 0.2, 2: 0.3, 3: 0.4} makes class 3 rows four times noisier than class 0 rows. It has no effect on which rows are noisy.

In short: selector = who is affected, noise_std_per_class = how badly.

docs.title: Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶
docs.text: CausalNoiseGenerator injects noise at a node of a fitted causal model. The noise perturbs the node's value, and the change cascades to the descendants through the structural equations: descendant = f(new parent values) + fresh noise. Only downstream nodes are affected; upstream nodes and untouched rows stay as they were.

docs.title: 1. Build the causal graph¶
docs.text: We use a three-node chain X -> Y -> Z. The node names are symbolic; a column_mapping maps them to column positions of X.

docs.title: 2. Generate data from the DAG¶
docs.text:
Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

Each node is a weighted sum of its parents plus noise, so the data already carries the causal structure the generator will exploit.

docs.title: 3. Fit the DGP¶
docs.text: The GcmSCMDGP adapter wraps a dowhy.gcm.StructuralCausalModel: every non-root node's mechanism is a linear AdditiveNoiseModel fitted on the original data, root nodes resample the observed values. The SCM is built with dowhy-gcm's own API (see the make_scm helper).

docs.title: 4. Inject causally-propagated noise¶
docs.text: We perturb node Y and watch the noise propagate to Z (but not to X).

docs.title: Expanding rows (n_copies)¶
docs.text: Set n_copies > 1 to expand the data: each original row produces n_copies noisy copies. Shape grows (appending mode).

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Lever Generator Uses a DGP? Propagates? Selector support observation process AdditiveNoiseGenerator no no (values only) — observation process, per class GaussianNoiseClassesGenerator no no (values only) ClassSelector DGP CausalNoiseGenerator yes (fitted) yes — descendants re-evaluated yes
  • Noise is row-wise: each affected row draws its own deviation — in contrast to drift, where one systematic shift hits all rows.
  • selector = who is affected (masks/probabilities per class), noise_std_per_class = how strongly (magnitude per class).
  • Causal noise mutates X in place — pass X.copy() to keep the original.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Shape is preserved: noise changes values only, never the row count.
  • AdditiveNoiseGenerator adds raw draws from any frozen scipy distribution; the scale is absolute (pass per-column scales yourself).
  • Causal noise recomputes descendants of the perturbed nodes via the DGP — the defect spreads through the graph.

# ============================================================
# Helper functions for the topology examples
# ============================================================

def generate_linear_data(graph, n_samples=100, rng=None, coefficients=None):
    """Generate data from a linear structural equation model defined by a DAG.

    Each edge (u -> v) has a coefficient w_uv. Node values are computed as:
        v = sum_{u in parents(v)} w_uv * u + noise
    where noise ~ N(0, 1).

    Parameters
    ----------
    graph : nx.DiGraph
        The causal DAG. Node names must be strings.
    n_samples : int
        Number of samples to generate.
    rng : np.random.Generator, optional
        Random number gen.
    coefficients : dict, optional
        Edge coefficients. Defaults to 1.0 for all edges.

    Returns
    -------
    X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_nodes)
    column_mapping : dict[str, int]
    """
    if rng is None:
        rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    if coefficients is None:
        coefficients = {edge: 1.0 for edge in graph.edges()}

    nodes = list(graph.nodes())
    node_to_idx = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)}
    n_nodes = len(nodes)

    X = np.zeros((n_samples, n_nodes))
    topo_order = list(nx.topological_sort(graph))

    for node in topo_order:
        idx = node_to_idx[node]
        parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
        if not parents:
            # Exogenous node: pure noise
            X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples)
        else:
            # Endogenous node: weighted sum of parents + noise
            X[:, idx] = rng.normal(size=n_samples)
            for parent in parents:
                parent_idx = node_to_idx[parent]
                coef = coefficients.get((parent, node), 1.0)
                X[:, idx] += coef * X[:, parent_idx]

    column_mapping = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(nodes)}
    return X, column_mapping

def plot_data(X, labels, column_names):
    """Scatter-matrix of the data with outliers highlighted in red.

    Parameters
    ----------
    X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features)
    labels : array-like or None
        Labels: "original" or "outliers". If None, all points are "original".
    column_names : list of str
        Names for each column.
    """
    is_outlier = np.asarray(labels) == "outliers" if labels is not None else np.zeros(len(X), dtype=bool)
    d = len(column_names)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(d, d, figsize=(2.5 * d, 2.5 * d))
    for i in range(d):
        for j in range(d):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            if i == j:
                # diagonal: histogram of the original data
                ax.hist(X[~is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C0", alpha=0.7)
                if is_outlier.any():
                    ax.hist(X[is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C3", alpha=0.7)
                ax.set_ylabel("Count") if j == 0 else ax.set_yticklabels([])
            elif i > j:
                ax.set_visible(False)  # hide lower triangle
            else:
                # upper triangle: scatter + regression line on original data
                ax.scatter(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], color="C0", s=15, alpha=0.6)
                ax.scatter(X[is_outlier, j], X[is_outlier, i], color="C3", s=30, alpha=0.6)
                if (~is_outlier).sum() > 1:
                    coef = np.polyfit(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], 1)
                    xs = np.array([X[~is_outlier, j].min(), X[~is_outlier, j].max()])
                    ax.plot(xs, coef[0] * xs + coef[1], color="C0", linewidth=1, alpha=0.5)
            if i == d - 1:
                ax.set_xlabel(column_names[j])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_ylabel(column_names[i])
    fig.suptitle("Data scatter-matrix (red = outliers)", y=1.02, fontsize=13)
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig

Parameters ---------- X : np.ndarray of shape (n_samples, n_features) labels : array-like or None Labels: "original" or "outliers". If None, all points are "original". column_names : list of str Names for each column. """ is_outlier = np.asarray(labels) == "outliers" if labels is not None else np.zeros(len(X), dtype=bool) d = len(column_names) fig, axes = plt.subplots(d, d, figsize=(2.5 * d, 2.5 * d)) for i in range(d): for j in range(d): ax = axes[i, j] if i == j: # diagonal: histogram of the original data ax.hist(X[~is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C0", alpha=0.7) if is_outlier.any(): ax.hist(X[is_outlier, j], bins=25, color="C3", alpha=0.7) ax.set_ylabel("Count") if j == 0 else ax.set_yticklabels([]) elif i > j: ax.set_visible(False) # hide lower triangle else: # upper triangle: scatter + regression line on original data ax.scatter(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], color="C0", s=15, alpha=0.6) ax.scatter(X[is_outlier, j], X[is_outlier, i], color="C3", s=30, alpha=0.6) if (~is_outlier).sum() > 1: coef = np.polyfit(X[~is_outlier, j], X[~is_outlier, i], 1) xs = np.array([X[~is_outlier, j].min(), X[~is_outlier, j].max()]) ax.plot(xs, coef[0] * xs + coef[1], color="C0", linewidth=1, alpha=0.5) if i == d - 1: ax.set_xlabel(column_names[j]) if j == 0: ax.set_ylabel(column_names[i]) fig.suptitle("Data scatter-matrix (red = outliers)", y=1.02, fontsize=13) plt.tight_layout() return fig In [25]: Copied! 
def draw_graph(graph, title=None):
    """Draw a DAG with fixed left-to-right node positions.

    Nodes are placed in topological generations: roots at x = 0, their
    descendants at x = 1, and so on; siblings are stacked vertically.
    This keeps the visual layout deterministic and consistent across
    all notebooks (no force-directed layout).
    """
    generations = {}  # node -> column index
    for node in nx.topological_sort(graph):
        parents = list(graph.predecessors(node))
        generations[node] = 0 if not parents else max(generations[p] for p in parents) + 1
    columns = {}
    pos = {}
    for node, col in generations.items():
        pos[node] = (col, columns.setdefault(col, 0))
        columns[col] += 1
    # center each column vertically
    height = max(columns.values())
    pos = {node: (x, y - (columns[x] - 1) / 2) for node, (x, y) in pos.items()}
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, figsize=(6, 2))
    nx.draw(graph, pos, ax=ax, node_color="lightblue", node_size=800, arrowsize=15)
    nx.draw_networkx_labels(graph, pos, ax=ax)
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.axis("off")
    return fig

def make_scm(graph):
    scm = gcm.StructuralCausalModel(graph)
    for node in graph.nodes:
        if not list(graph.predecessors(node)):
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.EmpiricalDistribution())
        else:
            scm.set_causal_mechanism(node, gcm.AdditiveNoiseModel(
                prediction_model=gcm.ml.create_linear_regressor()))
    return scm

docs.title: Generating outliers¶
docs.text:
Outliers are appended data points: the generator samples new rows that look extreme relative to the given data, and stacks them after the original rows — so Xt is larger than X. Use outliers to test how pipelines behave when rare, extreme observations appear: robust statistics, anomaly detection, scaling, and model fitting all react very differently to them.

This notebook shows the two levers available in badgers:

  1. Acting on the observation process — sample outliers directly from a distribution fitted to the data: one generic OutlierSamplingGenerator plus a pluggable out-of-distribution sampler (z-score, hypersphere, histogram and low-density). This generator does not use a DGP.
  2. Acting on the data-generating process (DGP) — perturb a node of a fitted causal model; the perturbation propagates to the descendants, so the outliers are not just extreme — they are structurally consistent extreme events (CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator).

Labels: the generated rows are the last rows appended to Xt (the count is set by the selector's count); the boolean array is exposed via get_outliers_labels().

docs.title: Goal¶
docs.text: Generate out-of-distribution points in tabular data — sampled directly from the data's own geometry (Part A) or propagated along a causal graph (Part B) — and identify which rows are outliers.

docs.title: Load and prepare data¶
docs.text: We first load an existing dataset from sklearn.datasets.

docs.title: Part A — Acting on the observation process (no DGP)¶
docs.text: OutlierSamplingGenerator samples outlier rows from a distribution or density derived directly from the data — the strategy is chosen by the out-of-distribution sampler passed to generate() (a registry name or a sampler instance from badgers.core.sampling). No causal model is involved; the outliers are marginal extremes, unrelated to any structure between the columns. The required CountSelector owns the count of appended rows (count) and the columns to perturb.

docs.title: Generate outliers using z-score sampling¶
docs.text: The "zscore" sampler (ZScoreSampler) generates points whose z-score (distance to the mean, in units of the standard deviation) exceeds 3 — far out on the tails of the empirical distribution.

docs.title: Generate outliers using hypersphere sampling¶
docs.text: The "hypersphere" sampler (HypersphereSampler) generates points uniformly on a hypersphere (a shell around the data) — extreme in every direction, not only along single axes.

docs.title: Generate outliers using independent histogram sampling¶
docs.text: The "independent_histogram" sampler (IndependentHistogramSampler) fits a histogram to each column independently, then samples outliers from the empty (or rare) bins — combinations that never occur in the data.

docs.title: Generate outliers using histogram sampling¶
docs.text: The "histogram" sampler (JointHistogramSampler) works on the joint histogram of the data — but only for low-dimensional datasets (the bin count explodes with dimensionality).

docs.title: Generate outliers using low density sampling¶
docs.text: The "low_density" sampler (KernelDensitySampler) samples points in the low-density regions of the empirical distribution — between and beyond the clusters, rather than at the extremes of single columns. It is a grid-CDF construction with no rejection step: a bounded regular grid (sized by grid_budget) is scored once with a kernel density estimate, and points are drawn from a categorical over the low-density grid cells — the generator always appends exactly selector.count points, deterministically for a fixed seed.

docs.title: Generate outliers using tree sampling¶
docs.text: The "tree" sampler (TreeCellSampler) is an adaptive histogram — no kernel density estimate: recursive median splits partition the data into cells holding at most leaf_size points, so the resolution is fine in dense regions and coarse in sparse ones. Every cell is extended axis-aligned across the full gap to the nearest data point on each side (the outermost cells reach the data-box boundary), so the leaves tile the whole box; a bounded coverage grid then finds every box region not covered by any leaf and adds it as an always-qualifying empty cell, so the space around and between the clusters is reachable as well. Points are drawn from a categorical over the cells whose extended-territory density is at most threshold_low_density times the global mean density, weighted by cell volume — the generator always appends exactly selector.count points.

docs.title: Generate outliers in a reduced space (decomposition + sampling)¶
docs.text: For higher-dimensional data, a first step is to reduce the dimensionality (any sklearn transformer with transform/inverse_transform, e.g. PCA, KernelPCA, FastICA) and sample outliers in the reduced space: StructuredOutlierGenerator chains a decomposition and an outlier sampler — outliers are sampled where the data really has little support, in the informative subspace rather than the noisy one.

docs.title: Part B — Acting on the data-generating process (DGP)¶
docs.text:
CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator perturbs a node of a fitted causal model with do()-style intervention: the node is set to an extreme value and the descendants are recomputed through the structural equations. The result: outliers that are extreme and structurally consistent — unlike Part A's marginal extremes, these respect the relationships between the columns.

The choice of perturbed node matters, and the topology decides how far the effect reaches — that is what the following examples show.

docs.title: Chain: \(X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z\)¶
docs.text: Perturbing X affects Y (direct child) and Z (indirect child). Perturbing Y affects Z but not X. The propagation direction is always downstream.

docs.title: Fork (common cause): \(C \rightarrow X, C \rightarrow Y\)¶
docs.text: Perturbing the common cause C moves both children X and Y — the outliers appear correlated even though the perturbation hit a single node.

docs.title: Sampling strategy comparison¶
docs.text: The within_distribution_sampler and out_of_distribution_sampler parameters control how the outlier values are drawn at the perturbation node:

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
Lever Generator Uses a DGP? Propagates? Effect on shape observation process OutlierSamplingGenerator + "zscore" / "hypersphere" / "uniform" sampler no no appends the selector's count rows observation process OutlierSamplingGenerator + "independent_histogram" / "histogram" / "low_density" sampler no no appends the selector's count rows observation process + decomposition StructuredOutlierGenerator no no appends (sampling happens in the reduced space) DGP CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator yes (fitted) yes — descendants re-evaluated appends perturbed + propagated rows
  • Outliers are an appending deficit: Xt is larger than X, and the generated rows are the last rows (one per selected seed row).
  • Outlier labels come from get_outliers_labels().
  • Part A's outliers are marginal extremes; Part B's outliers are structurally consistent extreme events whose footprint depends on the causal topology (chain / fork / collider / diamond).

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Outlier generators add rows beyond the data's distribution; the output has MORE rows than the input.
  • generate(X, **params) returns the single generated object Xt; the outlier flags come from gen.get_outliers_labels().
  • The causal variant (CausalOutlierPropagationGenerator) injects outliers at graph nodes and propagates them to descendants (Pearl surgery).

Imported by the notebooks in this directory via ``from _shared import ...``.
Kept as a plain module (leading underscore) so it stays out of the docs build.
